point: Free official filing systems for every listed-company deal in Japan (EDINET), the US (EDGAR) and the main Asian exchanges, plus exactly one paid licence (Tracxn, pending evaluation) for private deals and company profiles in the US and Asia.
evidence: See sheets 'Core sources deep dive' and 'Asia free bonus'.

section: Why the free sources are not a compromise
point: Regulators force listed companies to disclose acquisitions, mergers, tender offers and 5% stakes within days. The filings are the primary source that every commercial database copies from. Using them directly gives complete listed-company coverage, dated to the day, with no vendor lock-in and no redistribution problem.
evidence: EDGAR full-text search since 2001 and index since 1993; EDINET annual reports about 10 years; OpenDART from 1999. Commercial vendors cite these filings as their own sources.

point: It is the statutory system of record for about 5,100 annual-report filers (3,820 listed, 1,280 large unlisted), free, with an official API and permissive public-data terms. Extraordinary reports (臨時報告書) are viewable for 5 years and, for acquisitions above 15% of net assets, must state the target's name, address, capital, three years of results, purpose and consideration: a complete deal record. Annual reports (10 years) add the business-combination notes for every acquisition including smaller ones. The EDINET code list also gives the securities-code and corporate-number crosswalk that entity resolution needs.
evidence: Deep dive confirmed from the API spec v2.9 and FIEA Art. 25, 27-14, 27-28: annual / semi-annual / quarterly reports 10 years; extraordinary reports, tender-offer filings and 5% reports 5 years; list API accepts dates back 10 years. No source, free or paid, offers more than 5 years of Japanese M&A filings, so the archive must be built now.

point: The richest free M&A source in the world: 8-K Items 1.01 and 2.01, S-4, tender-offer and 13D filings, XBRL business-combination facts, all as JSON APIs and nightly bulk files with no key. It also captures US-listed Asian issuers and any Asian target bought by a US-listed company.
evidence: SEC developer resources: 10 requests/second, User-Agent rule, bulk submissions and companyfacts zips.

section: Why one paid licence and why Tracxn (with eyes open)
point: Private-to-private deals never appear in filings. One database that combines deal records and company profiles fills that hole without a second integration. Tracxn sells API, SFTP, Snowflake and BigQuery delivery priced by data scope rather than seats, and has a free Lite tier to measure recall before signing. Its published counts show where it is strong and weak: about 99,000 US acquisitions and 1.9M US companies, versus about 14,500 acquisitions across all of Asia (6% of its total), of which India is 5,600, China 1,900 and Japan 1,260. Korea, Taiwan and Hong Kong have no published counts. APAC outside India is 9% of its revenue. Conclusion: Tracxn is a strong US and India private-deal source and a weak one for East Asia. It is still the best single low-to-mid licence for 'US plus Asia', but East Asian private deals will remain thin whatever vendor is chosen at this budget.
evidence: Tracxn geography pages and FY26 annual report, captured in 'Core sources deep dive'. Decision gate: recall test on 50 known deals (weighted to Asia) before any commitment; fallback is Mergr for the US plus the free Asian exchange feeds.

point: Capital IQ, Orbis M&A, Refinitiv, PitchBook and Mergermarket have deeper private-deal history, but with API or feed rights they sit above USD 50k per year, and seat-only subscriptions forbid systematic extraction. The proposed stack delivers the listed-company core for free and reserves budget for the one private-deal gap.
evidence: Pricing rows in sheet 'Providers' (all quote-only, inferred enterprise tier).

point: Month 1: Japanese filings archived daily, US 8-K deals flowing. Month 2: ten-year Japanese acquisition history from annual reports, US history from 2001. Month 3: Korea and Taiwan feeds, Tracxn go / no-go with measured recall, unified deal database. Month 4: weekly lead lists in Salesforce.

Licences: EDINET, EDGAR, OpenDART, TWSE, gBizINFO, NTA API all JPY 0. Tracxn: quote, expected mid tier (its account base suggests few contracts above USD 36k-48k per year). Optional Japan complement at month 3: TDnet API at JPY 70,000 per month base plus metered fees up to JPY 340,000 per month, or TDnet on Snowflake full feed at JPY 340,000 per month for a single entity (the index-only tier is cheaper). Effort: roughly 20 person-weeks of engineering over four months, then part-time operations.
evidence: Cost column in 'Implementation plan'; TDnet prices from the JPX paid-data pages captured in the deep dive.

point: (1) Japanese M&A filings are viewable for only 5 years and Taiwan's TWSE feed is a same-day snapshot: start the archivers in week 1 so history accumulates. (2) Parsing Japanese and English filing text is the real work: budget it, start with rule-based extraction on a few document types; EDGAR's submissions API already exposes 8-K item numbers, which removes most US parsing. (3) Unofficial Asian endpoints (CNINFO, BSE, SGX) can break and HKEXnews needs a headless browser: treat as bonus, monitor. (4) Tracxn is thin on East Asian deals: the recall test decides before money is spent. (5) China cross-border data-transfer rules and Korea's KOGL Type 2 datasets (commercial use restricted) need legal review before ingestion.
evidence: Limitations columns in the deep-dive sheets.

section: A free bonus for unlisted Japan
point: The National Tax Agency corporate-number API records a closure cause and a successor corporate number for every company dissolved by merger since 2015. That is a free, threshold-free trail of Japanese mergers including unlisted-to-unlisted ones, with no deal terms but with the parties and the date. It should be part of the entity-resolution phase.
evidence: NTA Web API fields captured in 'Core sources deep dive'.

point: Acquisitions (as opposed to mergers) between two unlisted companies, especially Japanese SME succession deals, and most East Asian private deals. Those remain the firm's own deal flow and, if later needed, a Japanese commercial database (MARR Pro or SPEEDA RECOF), Tokyo Shoko Research company data, or regional databases (ITjuzi for China, DeepSearch for Korea).
